strengths: Novel empirical analysis of DPO/SimPO performance-stability tradeoff: Provides valuable evidence that KL regularization strength (β) creates fundamental tension between training stability and peak performance, with compelling learning rate sweep results

Exceptional experimental rigor and reproducibility: Comprehensive setup documentation (2,800 GPU hours), multiple evaluation frameworks, detailed hyperparameter specifications, and code release commitment enable full reproducibility

Strong practical data-efficiency results: Achieves 83.1% MATH-500 with 131k open examples vs 83.2% for DeepSeek-R1-Distill on 800k proprietary data, demonstrating significant practical value for practitioners

Thorough empirical validation: Pass@1 and pass@16 metrics across 5 benchmarks with error bars; ablation studies on α parameter; qualitative case study (Appendix E.2) showing improved error recovery; training dynamics analysis

Well-motivated and clearly presented methodology: Two-stage framework is intuitive; good use of figures to illustrate training dynamics; comprehensive appendices with convergence proof and additional analyses
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: REDI loss (Eq. 5) is straightforward α-weighted combination; asymmetric weighting is a simple heuristic rather than principled innovation; contribution is primarily empirical engineering rather than algorithmic advance

Severely constrained evaluation scope: Only 1.5B model tested (no evaluation on 7B, 13B, larger models); only mathematical reasoning domain; only one open dataset (OpenR1-Math); only one base model (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B) - limits generalizability claims substantially

Incomplete understanding of why negative examples help: Limited mechanistic analysis of what information negatives provide; case study (E.2) is anecdotal; no systematic error-type analysis; no exploration of negative selection strategies (multiple vs single negatives, hard negatives)

Key comparison fairness concerns: Table 1 DeepSeek comparison uses different training data (131k vs 800k) without controlled experiment; evaluation setup detail that '<think>' first token used for REDI models but unclear if applied consistently across all baselines, potentially introducing subtle biases

Modest primary benchmark improvements: MATH-500 shows 83.1% (REDI) vs 83.2% (DeepSeek) - within margin of error (±0.3 SEM); improvements of 0.6 points on average (Table 2) from best baselines are incremental

Technical gaps: Convergence proof assumes L-smoothness without verification for LLM loss functions; convergence analysis lacks details; token entropy analysis (Appendix F) suggests REDI may amplify existing patterns rather than improve robust reasoning; limited ablations on data sensitivity or negative quality

strengths: Rigorous empirical analysis of DPO/SimPO performance-stability tradeoff with controlled experiments (Figures 3-4), providing valuable insights for practitioners
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (MATH-500, AIME24, AMC23, Minerva, OlympiadBench) with proper error bars and systematic ablations
Strong practical results demonstrating data efficiency: Qwen-REDI-1.5B trained on 131k traces matches DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B trained on 800k proprietary data
Generalization validated across different architectures (Llama-3.2, Qwen-7B), scales, and out-of-domain tasks (GPQA +26.8%, HumanEval +181.2%)
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, computational accounting, training procedures, and data curation methods enabling full reproduction
Qualitative analysis (case study E.2) provides useful intuition about improved self-correction and error recovery capabilities
Theoretical grounding through β→0 limit analysis of SimPO converging to REINFORCE objective, with convergence guarantees in Appendix A
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: asymmetric weighting (Eq. 5) is conceptually straightforward; paper itself acknowledges asymmetric tuning as known heuristic, making contribution primarily empirical validation rather than innovation

Incomplete theoretical justification for asymmetric weighting—why α=0.8 specifically? The jump from symmetric (Eq. 4) to asymmetric (Eq. 5) objectives lacks principled motivation beyond empirical observation

Data efficiency claim based on single comparison point (131k vs 800k) with different base/teacher models; missing ablation on dataset size scaling and systematic evidence that 6× data reduction generalizes

Training instability not fully resolved: α=0.8 works well but symmetric α=1.0 still collapses with high learning rates; instability is mitigated rather than solved, and learning rate tuning remains critical

Limited analysis of negative trace value: no investigation of error type distribution, difficulty levels, or diversity impact; single-negative-per-problem strategy is pragmatic but potentially suboptimal
Narrow evaluation scope: mathematical reasoning only with brief out-of-domain tests; all traces from single teacher (Open-R1); generalization to other domains and teacher models unclear

Figure 10's finding that REDI amplifies existing token probability tendencies raises concerns about whether improvements represent genuine reasoning gains or mere distribution shifts without deeper analysis
Mixed pass@16 results (Table 6 shows AMC23 decrease from 90.4% to 81.9%) weakens claim that method preserves solution diversity; modest improvements on several benchmarks
Figure 8 generation statistics show small changes in token count and 'Wait' frequency with unclear significance and unexplored relationship to performance gains
Convergence guarantee (Appendix A) uses standard L-smoothness assumptions without specific analysis of why REDI is more stable than alternatives

strengths: Addresses practical problem of data efficiency in reasoning distillation through systematic utilization of negative traces
Thorough empirical analysis of performance-stability tradeoff in DPO/SimPO with clear visualizations of training dynamics
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks, architectures, and out-of-domain tasks with extensive ablations
Impressive data efficiency result: achieves performance comparable to model trained on 6.1× more data (131k vs 800k traces)
Well-documented reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, computational requirements, and training procedures
Strong and consistent experimental validation with pass@16 analysis confirming maintained solution diversity
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: asymmetric weighting is a minor hyperparameter modification to existing preference optimization methods
Weak theoretical justification for the proposed approach: no principled explanation for why α=0.8 is optimal or how to select α for new settings
Overstated novelty claim: DPO and SimPO already use both positive and negative traces; β→0 analysis is mathematical observation rather than deep insight
Modest performance improvements on absolute benchmarks (1-3% on most tasks, 0% on AMC23), with main story being data efficiency rather than reasoning capability gains

Experimental design conflates SFT improvements with method improvements: uses SFT-5ep for final model but SFT-3ep for baselines, making it unclear whether gains come from REDI or just better SFT initialization
Incomplete dataset utilization: single negative trace per problem for 'simplicity'; no experiments exploring multiple negatives despite potentially leaving performance gains on the table
Limited mechanistic understanding: single case study, modest generation statistics changes, and token-level analysis don't clearly explain how negative traces improve reasoning
Hyperparameter sensitivity: extensive tuning of all methods raises questions about whether improvements reflect method superiority or favorable tuning choices for REDI

strengths: Rigorous empirical methodology with extensive ablation studies (Figs 3-7, Tables 2, 4) demonstrating performance-stability tradeoffs and careful validation of design choices
Impressive data efficiency: Qwen-REDI-1.5B (131k traces) matches DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (800k proprietary traces), representing 6.1x improvement in sample efficiency
Excellent reproducibility: comprehensive experimental setup (Appendix C), detailed hyperparameter ranges, documented computational costs (2,800 A100 GPU hours), and promised code release

Thorough supplementary analysis including qualitative case studies (Appendix E.2) showing recovery from reasoning errors, pass@16 preservation analysis (Tables 6-7), token-level entropy analysis (Figures 9-10), and cross-architecture generalization (Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-Math-7B)
Simple and practical method: asymmetric weighting is straightforward to implement, making it easily adoptable by practitioners
Formal convergence guarantee under L-smoothness assumptions (Appendix A) provides theoretical grounding
Out-of-domain transfer (26.8% improvement on GPQA, 181.2% on HumanEval) suggests learned reasoning capabilities generalize beyond math domain
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification for asymmetric weighting mechanism: the paper relies heavily on citations (Yan et al., 2025b; Razin et al., 2025) without providing first-principles explanation of why α < 1 specifically stabilizes training or achieves better peak performance; convergence proof is standard and doesn't illuminate the asymmetric weighting advantage

Narrow evaluation scope: all primary benchmarks (MATH-500, AIME24, AMC23, Minerva, OlympiadBench) focus on mathematical reasoning; out-of-domain results (GPQA, HumanEval) are limited; no evaluation on other reasoning domains (logical reasoning, planning, commonsense, multi-hop QA)

Apples-to-oranges comparison with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: different teacher models, data pipelines, and filtering criteria make it difficult to isolate method contribution from data quality differences

Insufficient analysis of negative example characteristics: no investigation of which error patterns are most valuable, whether multiple negatives per problem could help, or how error types affect learning

Hyperparameter sensitivity under-addressed: learning rate appears highly sensitive; recommendation to fix α = 0.8 lacks principled guidance; unclear if optimal α generalizes across datasets/models/domains

Limited mechanistic understanding: Figure 10 shows token LogP correlation suggesting the method amplifies existing model tendencies rather than learning qualitatively new reasoning; acknowledged in Appendix F but not deeply analyzed
Limited novelty of core contribution: asymmetric weighting is straightforward; using negative examples in learning isn't new; concurrent work (Zhu et al., 2025) demonstrates similar motivations
Missing comparisons: no evaluation against alternative weighting schemes, recent preference optimization variants (IPO), or stronger rejection sampling baselines
Insufficient failure case analysis: no discussion of when REDI underperforms, which problem types or error distributions cause issues, or method boundaries
Key results presented in appendices: pass@16 analysis crucial for solution diversity claims should be in main text; cross-architecture results (Table 4) important for generalization claims
